opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difference comes down to where the ground truth lives.

In physics, the final judge is always nature. You can build a beautiful model, and AI can help you fit data, find patterns, and even suggest new equations. But in the end you have to go back to experiment. That loop is slow and expensive, and the data is noisy. So AI in physics is often about speeding up simulation, compressing huge datasets, or acting as a surrogate for calculations that would otherwise take enormous computing time. It helps us explore, but it doesn't replace the experiment that tells us whether we're right.

Mathematics is different because the truth is internal. A proof is either correct or it isn't, and with formal systems like Lean you can check that mechanically. That gives you something very valuable for AI: a clean, unambiguous reward signal. The model proposes a step, the verifier says yes or no, and you can iterate millions of times without building a particle accelerator. That's why we've seen such rapid progress in AI for math recently. The feedback loop is fast and essentially free of noise.

But there's a flip side. In physics, intuition about the real world constrains the search. You know roughly what kind of answer makes sense physically. In mathematics, the search space is enormous and much less constrained, and deciding which questions are worth asking, which definitions are the right ones, is still very much a human art. AI is getting good at proving things. It's much less clear that it knows what's interesting to prove.

So I'd put it this way: in physics, AI is a powerful assistant bottlenecked by contact with reality. In mathematics, verification is no longer the bottleneck, and the real frontier is taste — choosing the right problems and the right abstractions. That's where I think the most interesting collaboration between humans and AI will happen over the next few years.

r001.rationale: It says mathematical truth is internal and mentions formal systems like Lean, but does not state that mathematics operates entirely within a human-defined logical space.

r002.rationale: It says physics ultimately has to return to experiment and that experiments determine whether a model is right.

r003.rationale: It mentions physical models, simulation, and computational surrogates, but does not identify models of specialized phenomena such as fluid dynamics or aerodynamics as world models.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think the difference comes down to what counts as "truth" in each field.

In physics, the final arbiter is experiment. You can build a beautiful theory, but if the data disagrees, the data wins. So when you apply AI to physics, the model has an external ground truth it can be checked against, and that actually makes the problem a bit more forgiving. AI in physics is often about pattern recognition over very noisy, very high-dimensional data. Think about what we do in condensed matter: you have a twisted bilayer graphene device, you sweep gate voltage, magnetic field, temperature, and you get these enormous datasets. A huge part of the work is figuring out which features are real physics and which are artifacts of the sample. AI is very good at that kind of search, at suggesting "look here, something interesting is happening." It can also help with simulation, like solving many-body problems where the Hilbert space is too big for brute force. In that sense, AI in physics is often an accelerator for intuition. It points you somewhere, and then you go run the experiment.

Mathematics is almost the opposite. There is no experiment. The truth is internal to the logic, and a proof is either valid or it isn't. So the bar is much higher in one sense: the AI can't be "approximately right." A conjecture that's true in ninety-nine percent of cases is still false. But on the other hand, mathematics has something physics doesn't, which is formal verification. With systems like Lean, you can have a machine check every step. That's a very clean reward signal. You can let a model propose a proof, and you know with certainty whether it worked. Physics doesn't have that. Nature doesn't give you a green checkmark.

So I'd put it this way. In physics, AI's weakness is that the ground truth is expensive and messy, but its strength is that the problems are rich and the data is real. In mathematics, AI's weakness is that there's no tolerance for error, but its strength is that correctness can be verified mechanically, which makes it a natural fit for things like reinforcement learning.

And honestly, as an experimentalist, I find the physics side more humbling. A model can tell me the data suggests a new phase, but it can't tell me whether my sample is just dirty. That judgment, knowing what to trust, is still very much a human thing right now, probably more so than in math, where the verifier does a lot of that trusting for you.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematical truth is internal to logic, but does not state that mathematics operates entirely within a human-defined logical space.

r002.rationale: It says experiment is the final arbiter in physics and that a theory must be checked against data, with the experiment ultimately validating it.

r003.rationale: The response mentions physics data analysis and many-body simulation, but does not identify models of specialized physical phenomena as world models.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is what counts as a correct answer. In physics, ultimately you have to ask nature. You can have a beautiful model, and AI can help you build it, but if its predictions disagree with experiments, you have to revise it. In mathematics, you start with assumptions and ask what follows logically. The standard is a proof.

That gives AI somewhat different roles. In physics, it can help us find patterns in experimental data, speed up simulations, or identify promising experiments. And an approximation can be extremely useful, as long as we understand its accuracy and where it breaks down.

In mathematics, AI can also look for patterns and suggest conjectures. But checking a million examples doesn’t establish that something is always true. You still need the logical argument. If you express that argument in a formal system, a proof checker can verify it, which gives you a particularly clear way to test the AI’s output.

So I wouldn’t say one is necessarily easier. Physics has the challenge of connecting a model to a messy, partly observed world. Mathematics has the challenge of making every step of an argument hold. In both cases, finding an interesting pattern is only the beginning; the real work is establishing what you can trust.

r001.rationale: It says mathematics starts with assumptions and asks what follows logically, describing a human-defined logical framework.

r002.rationale: It says physical models must be checked against nature and revised if their predictions disagree with experiments.

r003.rationale: It mentions physics models, simulations, and experiments, but does not identify models of specialized physical phenomena as world models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is what counts as a successful answer. In physics, you’re trying to describe nature. You can use AI to find patterns in experimental data, build models, or suggest a new experiment, but ultimately you have to compare the prediction with what actually happens. A model can be useful even if it’s approximate, provided you understand where that approximation works.

In mathematics, finding a pattern is only the beginning. AI might notice that a statement holds in many examples and suggest a conjecture, but a million examples still don’t constitute a proof. You need a logical argument that establishes the result under the stated assumptions.

So in physics, AI has to connect with measurement; in mathematics, it has to connect with rigorous reasoning. In both cases, I think an exciting role is helping us discover something we wouldn’t have thought to look for. The challenge is turning that suggestion into something we can actually trust.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematics requires a proof under stated assumptions, but does not state that mathematics operates entirely within a human-defined logical space.
